opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think multimodality is one of the areas where there's still a lot of headroom, and it matters a lot in health because so much of medicine isn't purely text. A clinician looks at a rash, listens to how someone is breathing, reads an X-ray or an ECG, notices that a patient sounds confused or short of breath on the phone. Text-only models miss all of that context.

On images, models have gotten much better at general visual understanding, but there's a real gap between "can describe what's in a photo" and "can reliably interpret a skin lesion across different skin tones, lighting conditions, and phone cameras." Robustness and calibration are the big issues. In consumer settings people take blurry photos and crop out the relevant part, and the model needs to know when it can't make a confident call and should ask for a better image or suggest seeing someone in person. Specialized modalities like radiology, pathology slides, and retinal images also have very different statistics from natural images, so there's a lot of work to do on evaluation and on making sure performance holds up across populations and devices.

Voice is interesting in a different way. Part of it is accessibility: many people, especially older folks or people with lower literacy or who don't speak a dominant language, are much more comfortable talking than typing. A good voice experience could make health information far more accessible. But voice also carries clinical signal: how someone speaks, whether they're breathless, slurring, distressed. We should be careful about overclaiming there, but there's real potential, along with real privacy and consent questions.

Then there's the interaction design layer. In a voice conversation you can't throw up a long, nuanced answer with caveats and links. The model has to be concise, ask the right follow-up questions, prioritize what matters, and escalate appropriately if something sounds urgent. That's a different skill than producing a great written response, and I don't think we've fully figured out how to evaluate it yet.

So for me the room for improvement is less about raw capability and more about reliability, knowing what you don't know, equitable performance across people and conditions, and evaluations grounded in how people actually use these tools in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses medical imaging reliability and voice accessibility, but does not express hope that the best medical imaging models will also be the most readily accessible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a lot of room, honestly. If you look at how clinicians actually work, so much of medicine is multimodal. A dermatologist is looking at a lesion, a radiologist is reading a chest X-ray, a primary care doctor is listening to how a patient describes their symptoms and picking up on tone, hesitation, whether they sound short of breath. And for a long time, the models we built for health were really text-first. The language capabilities got good fast, and the image and audio side was sort of bolted on afterward.

So the first area is just depth of understanding in images. A lot of models can describe an image at a surface level, they can say "this looks like a rash" or "this is a chest X-ray." But the thing a clinician actually needs is the fine-grained reasoning: is this nodule concerning, how does it compare to the prior scan, what's the differential given this specific appearance plus the patient's history. That kind of grounded, comparative reasoning across modalities is still immature. And a lot of the public benchmarks don't really capture it, so it's easy to overestimate where we are.

The second piece is longitudinal and context-rich interpretation. Real health data isn't one image in isolation. It's a series of images over time, plus labs, plus notes, plus what the patient tells you. Models that can hold all of that together and reason about change over time, that's a big gap and a big opportunity.

On the voice side, I'd say we're even earlier. There's the obvious stuff, like transcription in clinical settings, ambient documentation, which is already useful. But the more interesting frontier is using voice as a signal itself. There's real evidence that things like respiratory conditions, some neurological conditions, even mental health states leave traces in how people speak. Capturing that in a way that's robust across accents, recording conditions, different devices, and especially across populations that are underrepresented in training data, that's hard and it's not solved.

And then I think the thing that cuts across both images and voice is the question of calibration and knowing when you don't know. In health, a confident wrong answer is much worse than an honest "I'm not sure, you should get this checked." The models need to be able to express uncertainty in a way that's actually useful to a clinician or a patient, and they need to be evaluated with real clinicians in the loop, not just on static datasets. That's the part I'd really push on: the evaluation has to be as multimodal and as grounded as the use case, otherwise we're flying blind about whether these systems are actually safe and helpful.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses gaps in medical image understanding and evaluation, but does not express hope that the best medical imaging models will be the most accessible to people.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of room for improvement in both. With images, it’s not enough for a model to describe what it sees. It needs to pick up on clinically meaningful details, connect those details to the patient’s history, and recognize when the image just doesn’t contain enough information to draw a conclusion. A model can give a very fluent explanation while missing the thing that matters, so we need to evaluate those capabilities carefully.

Voice is exciting because it can make interacting with these systems much more natural. Someone can explain what’s going on in their own words without having to type everything out. But the system has to handle accents, interruptions, and ambiguous descriptions, and know when to ask a follow-up question rather than assume it understood.

The bigger opportunity is bringing those inputs together. In health, an image or a conversation rarely stands alone. You want a system that can use the relevant context while being clear about what it knows and where it’s uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving medical image understanding, but does not express hope that the best imaging models will also be readily accessible to people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of room to improve both the underlying capabilities and how we evaluate them. With images, it’s not enough to do well on a benchmark where you’re given a clean image and asked a specific question. In practice, the image might be blurry, the relevant finding might be subtle, and you need the patient’s history to interpret it. A useful model needs to combine that information and recognize when it doesn’t have enough evidence to say something confidently.

With voice, there’s an opportunity to make these systems much more accessible. People can describe what’s going on in their own words, without having to type out a medical history. But the system needs to handle accents, interruptions, and medical terminology reliably, and ask good follow-up questions when something is unclear.

Across both, I’d want to see more evaluation in realistic clinical workflows. Does adding an image or a voice interaction actually help someone make a better decision? That’s a much more meaningful target than simply having the modality available.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving image models and making voice systems more accessible, but it does not express the hope that the best medical imaging models will also be the most accessible.
